heading: INT. COUNTY COURTHOUSE - DEFENSE ATTORNEY'S OFFICE - NIGHT

units.text: INT. COUNTY COURTHOUSE - DEFENSE ATTORNEY'S OFFICE - NIGHT
A narrow, windowless room lit by a green banker's lamp.
Case files tower on the desk.
A coffee ring has dried on a closing-argument draft.
A dictaphone sits by a cold sandwich.
THEODORA WREN, 50s, defense counsel, in a rumpled suit with her shoes off, paces between the desk and the file cabinet with a legal pad.
She stops, scribbles a line, crosses it out, tears the page off, crumples it, and throws it at the wastebasket.
It misses.
Behind her, through the glass door, the empty gallery waits with its rows of dark benches and the quiet of a held breath, and above it all the clock ticks past two.
Members of the jury.
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She shakes her head and tries again, lower.
Ladies and gentlemen. You have heard from forty witnesses.
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She stops.
She presses the heel of her hand to her eyes.
Then she sits, flicks on the dictaphone, and a red light glows.
Closing, version nine. Begin.
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She clears her throat.
Her voice drops into the cadence of a long-practiced speech.

Members of the jury. For three weeks, you've been told a story. You've been told it by a man in a good suit with a binder and a smile. And I want you to ask yourselves one question, only one: who benefits from this story being true?
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She stops the tape.
Rewinds.
Plays it back.
Who benefits from this story being true?
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She winces.
Stops it.
Lets out a long sigh.
Terrible.
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She goes to the file cabinet, pulls a drawer, and lifts out a thick folder.
She weighs it in her hands: the transcripts, the exhibits, the blood evidence, the long dull ledger of a case that began as a footnote and swallowed a year of her life.
She sets it on the desk and opens it to a photograph.
A young man, grinning, in a graduation cap.
She traces his face with a fingertip.
I don't know if you did it.
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She picks up the dictaphone.
New take. Members of the jury. I don't know if my client is innocent. I don't know. I've never known. And neither does the prosecutor, though he has spent three weeks pretending otherwise.
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She stops.
She stares at the red light.
She is shaking.

But I know this: a reasonable doubt is not a flaw in the law. It's the law's only conscience. And if there is a single one of you who cannot say, with a clear heart, that he did it, then you must say that he did not.
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: The light on the dictaphone stutters.
The tape runs out with a soft clack.
She sits in the sudden quiet, hand over her mouth, and in the empty gallery beyond the glass, a bench creaks as if someone, an old or invisible juror, has shifted to listen.
She lowers her hand.
Tears track down her face, and she wipes them with the back of her wrist, laughing a little.
That's the one.
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She rewinds the tape.
Plays it back.
...then you must say that he did not.
units.name: THEODORA

units.text: She nods, sets the dictaphone down, and for the first time that night, reaches for the cold sandwich.
